source.title: Action is All You Need: Dual-Flow Generative Ranking Network for Recommendation
source.authors: Hao Guo; Erpeng Xue; Lei Huang; Shi-Chao Wang; Xiaolei Wang; Lei Wang; Jin-Peng Wang; Sheng Chen

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study investigates scaling in a new setting: a generative recommendation ranking model, using G-AUC rather than language-model pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The study does not measure held-out language-model cross-entropy or sweep language-model parameters and tokens. It does report DFGR recommendation G-AUC against computational complexity and describes how the preferred depth changes with compute. The cited scaling-law results from other papers are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study fits its own scaling curve for a generative recommendation ranker (DFGR), plotting best G-AUC against training compute (Fig. 9). This is a new setting for V5. The evidence is weak: the measure is a bounded ranking metric rather than loss, the fit is log-linear, and compute spans under one order of magnitude.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors say DFGR follows a scaling law: best G-AUC rises linearly in log compute, which they call a power-law pattern. They also say deeper models become optimal as compute and data grow. Their main conclusion is that DFGR outperforms DLRM, MetaGR and other baselines while being more efficient.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales a recommendation ranking model and measures G-AUC against computational complexity; it does not use the original language-model held-out cross-entropy setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported preferred depth changes with computational complexity; the study compares five depth/width configurations.

fits_no_version.finding: At roughly matched compute, the best depth/width configuration shifts from 2 to 4 to 8 layers as compute grows. The 1-layer and 16-layer configurations underperform throughout.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In recommendation transformers, the compute-optimal depth/width ratio shifts toward deeper models as compute increases.

record.problems: The scaling result is reported for recommendation G-AUC, not held-out language-model cross-entropy. The scaling plot provides no stated uncertainty, and the text does not give numeric results for the plotted compute sweep.

untested.parts: Loss-based power laws; other modalities and training regimes (image, video, repeated data, fine-tuning); compute ranges over several orders of magnitude; separate scaling in parameters or data.
Not tested: no language-model pretraining loss.
Not tested: no extrapolation from small runs.
Not tested: no parameter/token optimal allocation.
Not tested: depth/width were varied at roughly equal compute, not at fixed parameter count.
Not tested: no comparison of fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: Main contribution is architectural. The scaling evidence is a single figure. The 'power-law' label is the authors' own; the actual fit is logarithmic. Peer reviewed (CIKM '25).

versions.untested_parts: No language-model held-out pretraining loss or power-law sweeps in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No extrapolation from smaller runs to substantially larger runs.
The study does not report loss-minimizing parameter counts and token counts as powers of compute.
Depth and width are varied under equivalent computational budgets, not at a fixed parameter count.
Only recommendation ranking with DFGR and G-AUC versus computational complexity is tested; other modalities and training regimes are not.
No downstream language-model task performance or relationship to pretraining loss is evaluated.
The study does not compare fitting choices or exponents, or test whether curves bend away from a power law.

rows.subject: DFGR
rows.operation_detail: Plots the G-AUC of optimal DFGR configurations against computational complexity.

conditions.value: not stated for this scaling plot
computational complexity in PetaFLOPs; plotted range and individual values are figure only

rows.value: Figure only; the paper describes G-AUC as improving linearly with computational complexity following a power-law pattern. The plotted fit is y = 0.0077*log(x) + 0.6774.
rows.note: This is recommendation ranking performance, not held-out language-model cross-entropy. The fit is reported as shown in the figure.
rows.check: The fit is G-AUC = 0.0077*log(x)+0.6774, a log-linear fit of a bounded ranking metric, not a power law in loss. Compute spans about 100–800 PetaFLOPs, under one order of magnitude. The points are the envelope of five training curves from Fig. 8 (best configuration at each compute level), not separately trained compute-optimal runs. Dataset is presumably TRec but not stated. No baseline or uncertainty is given.

rows.subject: DFGR
rows.operation_detail: Compares model depth and width configurations under equivalent computational budgets and describes which depths perform best as compute increases.

conditions.value: 1 layer / 360 units; 2 layers / 216 units; 4 layers / 120 units; 8 layers / 64 units; 16 layers / 32 units

rows.value: The 1-layer configuration is described as significantly inferior throughout training; the 16-layer configuration is suboptimal across training phases; among the remaining configurations, optimal depth shifts from 2 to 4 to 8 layers as computational expenditure increases.
rows.note: This reports a depth/width allocation trend, not parameter-count and token-count scaling or loss-minimizing allocations.
rows.check: The five configurations (1x360 to 16x32) differ in parameter count (roughly L*D^2, about 130k down to 16k in the attention blocks). The comparison is therefore not at a fixed parameter count (V4) and is not a parameter/token split (V3). It is correctly recorded under fits_no_version.

relationships.condition: DFGR generative recommendation ranking on industrial data, G-AUC vs training compute (about 100–800 PFLOPs)
relationships.reason: G-AUC rises steadily with compute, but the fit is log-linear in a bounded metric over less than one decade. It is built from an envelope of training curves, so the power-law form in loss is not shown (r1).
relationships.display_finding: G-AUC increased steadily across about 100–800 PFLOPs, with a log-linear fit to the training-curve envelope rather than a loss power law.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
